title: Running Route Planner: Plan Runs with GPX
description: Plan a running route on the pedestrian network with the Running Route Planner — distance, map line and GPX export for your watch. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a planned riverside 8.2 km with the distance known before the laces are tied — the session prescribed, measured and exportable.
quick_answer: The Running Route Planner creates a route between start and finish on the pedestrian network — streets and paths a runner can use — and reports its distance, drawn on the map. Plan the run, check the distance needed, and export GPX for your watch or phone.
steps_intro: A run planned is a run measured. Build it on the network runners are allowed:

body.t: The plan prescribes distance, not geography: build the route that delivers exactly the kilometres — loops are the
's craft when home is both ends.
Travel runs on unknown streets deserve a pedestrian-legal route and a known distance. This is the traveller's local knowledge, generated.
GPX is the runner's lingua franca: plan here, send the file, and the whole club runs the same line on Saturday.
An unfamiliar race town's training runs, planned before arrival — distances known, surfaces checkable in the
Route Surface and Road Type Finder
Training says 12 km easy. The planner iterates a route until its reported distance is the session's distance — the map bends to the plan, not the reverse.
Exported, the planned line becomes the watch's breadcrumb. The run you designed at the desk is the run your feet execute.

faq: Does it know every trail?
It knows the pedestrian network as OpenStreetMap records it — streets, paths and trails that mappers have drawn. Remote or new trails may be missing; coverage is the data's, stated plainly.
Is running speed included?
The planner reports distance; your pace turns it into time — the Pace to Speed Calculator converts, and the Hiking Pace tools measure your real pace on foot.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Runners share roads with traffic but are not routed by it; crossings are the runner's judgement, always.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
The pedestrian network winds like every network. The reported distance is the run's real length.
Can route results change over time?
Yes — new paths appear in the data and old ones get corrected. A cherished route deserves a fresh plan each season.
Can I export to my watch?
GPX export is built in, and GPX is the format watches and run apps import. Plan here, run there.
Point to point leaves me far from home.
Then the run is a journey — or generate a loop instead. Many runners plan one-way runs toward a train station on purpose.
Does it avoid main roads?
Pedestrian routing prefers paths and pavements where the data offers them; a road section appears when the network has no gentler link.
Can I plan interval sessions?
Plan the route for distance, then run the session on it — the planner measures the stage, your watch conducts the play.
My watch wants a different format.
GPX is the common tongue; if a device insists otherwise, its own app converts GPX happily.
